quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Cities are often several degrees warmer than the countryside around them. Dark roofs and asphalt soak up sunlight and release it slowly after sunset, while tall buildings block the wind that would carry heat away. With fewer trees to provide shade, the warmth builds up. On summer nights, this can keep residents from cooling down and sleeping well.
options: Cost of Building Very Tall Buildings
Sleeping Comfortably During a Summer Heat Wave
Why Cities Stay Hot After Sunset
How Trees Can Cool an Entire Neighborhood
quests.correctAnswer: Why Cities Stay Hot After Sunset
quests.hint: Look for the words that link one fact to the next. What leads to what?
quests.explanation: The passage is organized as a chain of causes: dark surfaces, blocked wind, and missing shade lead to lasting heat. A title that names only the solution or only the sleep problem skips the chain.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title names the effect, lingering heat, that all the listed causes combine to produce.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: The lunch queue at Haven Café stretched out the door, and customers were leaving before they ordered. The owner noticed that most of the delay came from taking payments at the same counter as orders. She added a second register for payments only and let regulars order through an app. Waits fell from fifteen minutes to five.
options: Letting Regulars Order Through an App
Cutting Lunch Waits at a Crowded Café Counter
Adding a Second Register
Why Customers Leave Long Lines
quests.correctAnswer: Cutting Lunch Waits at a Crowded Café Counter
quests.hint: Sort the passage into a problem, what was done, and what changed.
quests.explanation: The second register and the app are both parts of the solution, so each alone is too narrow. The best title covers the problem and the improvement together.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title combines the long queue with the changes that shortened it.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Paper books and e-readers each suit different readers. A paper book needs no battery and can be lent to a friend, but it takes space in a bag. An e-reader holds hundreds of titles in something thinner than a magazine and lets you adjust the text size. However, many readers say a printed page feels more restful, especially before sleep.
options: Why E-Readers Are Better for Travel
Paper Books and E-Readers: Strengths and Weaknesses
Future of Printed Books
How to Choose a Bedtime Story
quests.correctAnswer: Paper Books and E-Readers: Strengths and Weaknesses
quests.hint: Ask whether the writer favors one side or weighs both.
quests.explanation: The passage sets strengths and weaknesses of two formats next to each other. A title that praises one format ignores half of it.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice reflects the balanced comparison of the two reading formats.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Old newspapers begin their second life at a recycling plant. First, they are shredded and mixed with water to form a soft pulp. Next, screens remove staples and bits of plastic, and the pulp is cleaned with hot water. Finally, it is pressed flat between rollers and dried into new sheets.
options: Why Recycling Helps Protect Forests
The Long History of Printed News
Removing Staples with Screens
From Old Newspaper to New Sheets of Paper
quests.correctAnswer: From Old Newspaper to New Sheets of Paper
quests.hint: Words like first, next, and finally are clues to how the passage is built.
quests.explanation: The passage follows a sequence from old sheets to new ones. Removing staples is a single stage, and forests are never mentioned.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title covers the whole sequence, from the shredded start to the dried finish.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Living close to a train station has clear benefits. Commuting is quick, and shops and cafés tend to gather nearby. On the other hand, trains bring noise late at night and early in the morning, and rents are usually higher than on quieter streets. Whether it is worth it depends on how much a person values convenience over calm.
options: Weighing the Pros and Cons of Living by a Station
Why Rents Rise Near Stations
Convenience of a Short Commute
How to Choose a Quiet Neighborhood
quests.correctAnswer: Weighing the Pros and Cons of Living by a Station
quests.hint: Find the phrase 'on the other hand.' What does it do to the structure?
quests.explanation: The passage first gives advantages and then disadvantages, and it ends by leaving the choice to the reader. Each single-side title covers only one part.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title matches the two-sided structure and the closing point that the answer depends on the person.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: A phone's battery drains faster when many apps run in the background. Each one checks for updates, refreshes its data, and sometimes tracks location, so the processor rarely gets to rest. Screen brightness adds to the load. Closing unused apps and switching off location for those that do not need it can noticeably extend the day's charge.
options: Dimming the Screen to Save Battery Power on Long Days
Tracking Location with Apps
How Phone Batteries Are Manufactured
Draining and Saving Phone Battery Power
quests.correctAnswer: Draining and Saving Phone Battery Power
quests.hint: Notice that the passage explains a cause and then gives a response.
quests.explanation: Screen brightness and location tracking are two pieces of a larger explanation. The passage also offers ways to reduce the drain, which the title should include.
quests.whyThisTitle: It pairs the causes of battery drain with the remedies the passage ends on.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Parents dropping off children at Northfield Elementary caused a daily traffic jam that blocked the street and worried neighbors. The school responded with a 'walking bus': volunteers lead groups of children on foot from a meeting point ten minutes away. Within a semester, car arrivals dropped by a third, and the street was calmer.
options: Why So Many Parents Drive to School
How a Walking Bus Eased the School Traffic Jam
Neighbors Worried About Street Safety
Volunteers Leading Groups of Children on Foot
quests.correctAnswer: How a Walking Bus Eased the School Traffic Jam
quests.hint: What was wrong at the start, and what fixed it?
quests.explanation: The volunteers and the worried neighbors are pieces of the story. The passage links the traffic problem to the walking bus and its results.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title states the solution and the problem it addressed.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Renting and buying a home offer different kinds of security. Renters can move easily and are not responsible for major repairs, but they have less control over the space and may face rising rents. Owners build equity and can renovate freely, yet they carry the cost of repairs and are tied to one place. Neither option is better for everyone.
options: Renting or Buying a Home
Why Rents Keep Rising
Paying for Home Repairs
Saving Up for a First Home
quests.correctAnswer: Renting or Buying a Home
quests.hint: Ask whether the writer recommends one option.
quests.explanation: Rising rents and repairs are details on opposite sides of the comparison. The passage ends by refusing to pick a winner, which fits a title that stays neutral.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title covers both options and the final point that neither is best for everyone.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: In most places, getting a driver's license follows a set order. Applicants first pass a written test on road rules and receive a learner's permit. They then log practice hours with an adult, usually including some night driving. Only after that can they book the road test, and a passing score earns the license.
options: Earning a Driver's License
Why Young Drivers Have More Accidents
Passing a Written Test on Road Rules
Practicing Night Driving with an Adult
quests.correctAnswer: Earning a Driver's License
quests.hint: Which words tell you the order matters?
quests.explanation: The written test and night practice are stages inside a longer path. The sequence words first, then, and only after show that the whole process is the subject.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title names the full path from permit to license rather than one stage.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: When seawater grows too warm, corals push out the tiny algae that live inside them and give them color and food. Without the algae, the coral turns white, a condition called bleaching. A bleached coral is not dead, but it is weak and starving. If temperatures stay high for weeks, the coral may not recover, and the fish that depend on the reef lose their home.
options: Protecting Fish Homes in the Ocean
The Tiny Algae Living Inside Coral
Why Some Corals Look White
How Warm Water Harms Coral Reefs and Their Fish
quests.correctAnswer: How Warm Water Harms Coral Reefs and Their Fish
quests.hint: Trace the chain from the first event to the last.
quests.explanation: The white color, the algae, and the fish are links in one cause-and-effect chain. The title should name the starting cause and the harm it leads to.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice connects the warming water at the start with the damage at the end.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Many students take a part-time job while they study. The income covers living costs, and the job teaches punctuality and teamwork. But long shifts can leave little time for homework, and tiredness may lower grades. Students who work ten hours a week or fewer often report that they can balance both.
options: Earning Enough Money to Cover Living Costs
Finding a Job Near Campus
Working While Studying
Why Grades Fall During Exams
quests.correctAnswer: Working While Studying
quests.hint: The word 'but' marks a turn. What comes before it and after it?
quests.explanation: The passage lists benefits, then risks, then a condition under which balance is possible. A title about only money or only grades leaves out one side.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title covers the advantages and the drawbacks, which the passage gives in turn.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Overdue fines were supposed to make readers return books on time, but the city library found that the fines kept low-income families away entirely. The library ended fines and began sending text reminders three days before each due date. Late returns did not increase, and thousands of lapsed members came back.
options: Bringing Lapsed Members Back
Sending Text Messages to Readers
Replacing Library Fines with Reminders
Why Some Low-Income Families Avoid Public Libraries
quests.correctAnswer: Replacing Library Fines with Reminders
quests.hint: Ask what the library changed and why.
quests.explanation: Lapsed members returning and the text messages are separate pieces. The passage presents fines as the problem and reminders as the answer.
quests.whyThisTitle: It names the swap that resolved the problem the passage describes.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Coffee cherries are picked by hand when they are red. At the mill, the fruit is removed and the seeds are washed and dried in the sun for about two weeks. The dried beans are sorted, packed, and shipped to roasters, who heat them until they turn brown and develop flavor. Only then are they ground and brewed.
options: Picking Fruit by Hand
Why Coffee Grows in Warm Countries
Roasting Coffee Beans to Bring Out Their Flavor
The Long Journey from Coffee Cherry to Cup
quests.correctAnswer: The Long Journey from Coffee Cherry to Cup
quests.hint: What is the passage following from start to end?
quests.explanation: Roasting is one step, and the growing climate is never discussed. The passage follows the coffee through each stage until it is brewed.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title matches a chain of steps from the harvested fruit to the finished drink.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Some people keep a to-do list; others schedule their tasks into a calendar. A list is flexible and quick to update, but it does not show how long each task will take. A calendar forces you to face the limits of the day, though it can feel rigid when plans change. Many people combine the two, listing tasks and then placing the important ones in time slots.
options: Planning a Day with Lists or Calendars
Building a Habit of Writing Lists Every Day
Why Calendars Feel Too Rigid
Planning Meetings with Coworkers
quests.correctAnswer: Planning a Day with Lists or Calendars
quests.hint: Notice how the passage treats each method in turn and then brings them together.
quests.explanation: The rigidity of calendars is one downside of one method. The passage compares both and ends with a way to combine them.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title reflects the comparison and the closing suggestion that the two can work together.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Airfares climb during school holidays because many families want to travel on the same few days. Airlines know that seats will fill even at higher prices, so they raise them. Travelers with flexible dates often find lower fares by leaving mid-week or choosing a nearby airport. The extra cost is not a punishment; it is a response to crowded demand.
options: Finding Cheaper Flights by Leaving Mid-Week
How Airlines Choose Their Routes
Higher Flight Prices at Peak Times
Traveling with Children in the Summer
quests.correctAnswer: Higher Flight Prices at Peak Times
quests.hint: Ask which idea explains the pricing rather than reacts to it.
quests.explanation: Mid-week travel is a tip that follows from the explanation. The main line of the passage is why the price rises when demand rises.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice states the cause, crowded demand, and the effect on fares.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Useful feedback is specific. Rather than saying a report is confusing, point to the paragraph where the reader got lost and explain why. Mention what worked as well as what did not, so that the writer knows what to keep. Finally, offer one suggestion for improvement instead of a long list; too many changes at once are hard to act on.
options: Giving Feedback That Actually Helps
Writing Clear Reports for Business Readers
Why Criticism Is Hard to Accept
Praising a Coworker's Work
quests.correctAnswer: Giving Feedback That Actually Helps
quests.hint: The passage gives several pieces of advice. What skill are they all for?
quests.explanation: Praise is one small piece, and report writing is only the example. The passage teaches how to give feedback so it can be used.
quests.whyThisTitle: Being specific, balanced, and selective are all ways of making feedback useful.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Each autumn, the small clinic in Ridge Valley struggled to vaccinate older residents, many of whom lived far from town and had no car. This year, nurses parked a van in the village square for two afternoons. Almost three times as many people were vaccinated as the year before.
options: A Nurse's Van in the Village Square
Taking Flu Shots to Older Residents
Rising Numbers of Flu Cases Each Autumn
Why Older Residents Avoid Clinics
quests.correctAnswer: Taking Flu Shots to Older Residents
quests.hint: Locate the difficulty and the result of the new approach.
quests.explanation: The van is the method, and the avoidance of clinics is only a guess about the problem. The passage is really about the distance barrier and how moving the service solved it.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title expresses the change of location that produced the jump in vaccinations.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Rental electric scooters can be handy for short trips. They are quick, cheap, and free riders from traffic. Still, they are often left on sidewalks, where they block wheelchairs and prams, and injuries from falls have risen. Some cities now require designated parking spots, hoping to keep the convenience while reducing the harm.
options: The Promise and Problems of City Scooters
Designated Parking Spots for Rental Scooters
Riding Safely on Busy Sidewalks
Why Cities Ban Some Vehicles
quests.correctAnswer: The Promise and Problems of City Scooters
quests.hint: How many sides of the issue does the passage cover?
quests.explanation: Parking spots are one city response. The passage weighs benefits against harm and then mentions a partial fix.
quests.whyThisTitle: It captures both the appeal and the difficulties, which is what the passage presents.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: A new museum exhibit takes months to prepare. Curators begin by choosing a theme and finding objects that tell its story. Conservators then check each item for damage and repair what they can. Designers plan the lighting and layout, and writers prepare short labels. Only in the final week are the objects placed in their cases.
options: Work of Museum Conservators
Why Museums Need Careful Lighting and Layout
How a Museum Exhibit Comes Together
How to Choose a Theme for a Show
quests.correctAnswer: How a Museum Exhibit Comes Together
quests.hint: Which words show that the tasks happen in stages?
quests.explanation: The passage moves from choosing a theme to placing objects. Conservators and lighting are only stages within it.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title covers each stage of preparation, from theme to finished display.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Traffic sometimes stops for no visible reason. One driver taps the brake a little too hard, the driver behind brakes slightly harder, and the effect grows down the line until cars far back come to a complete halt. By the time the front car moves on, the delay has become a wave that travels backward. Keeping a longer gap between cars helps absorb these small taps.
options: Keeping a Longer Gap Between Moving Cars on Highways
Roadworks That Slow Traffic
The Danger of Rear-End Accidents
How One Brake Tap Causes a Traffic Jam
quests.correctAnswer: How One Brake Tap Causes a Traffic Jam
quests.hint: The passage starts with a puzzle. Which choice answers it?
quests.explanation: The longer gap is advice added at the end. The main body explains how a small action spreads into a jam.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title describes the chain reaction that the passage explains.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Cars with automatic gearboxes are easier to learn: the driver only steers, accelerates, and brakes. Manual cars ask learners to coordinate a clutch and a gear lever, which takes practice, but they often cost less to buy and repair. Many drivers who learn manual say they feel more involved in driving, while automatic drivers value the calm of stop-and-go traffic.
options: Buying a Car on a Budget
Automatic and Manual Cars Compared
Learning to Use a Clutch and Gear Lever
Driving Calmly in Heavy Traffic
quests.correctAnswer: Automatic and Manual Cars Compared
quests.hint: Are the two types of cars treated equally in the passage?
quests.explanation: The clutch, the cost, and the traffic are single points. The passage sets the two gearbox types against each other on several features.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title matches the point-by-point comparison of the two kinds of car.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: A strong password is long rather than complicated. A phrase of four or five unrelated words is harder for a program to guess than a short mix of symbols, and it is easier to remember. Use a different one for each important account, and store them in a password manager if you have many. Turn on a second check, such as a code sent to your phone, wherever it is offered.
options: Building Passwords That Are Hard to Break
Using a Password Manager
Remembering Long Phrases Without Writing Them Down
How Hackers Guess Passwords
quests.correctAnswer: Building Passwords That Are Hard to Break
quests.hint: Consider the purpose of every tip.
quests.explanation: The password manager and long phrases are two tips. The passage offers a set of ways to make accounts harder to break into.
quests.whyThisTitle: All the advice about length, uniqueness, and second checks serves the goal of stronger passwords.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Houseplants often lean toward a window. The reason is that plant cells on the shaded side grow faster than those on the sunlit side, which bends the stem toward the light. This helps the plant capture more sunlight. Turning the pot a quarter turn each week keeps growth even and prevents the plant from becoming lopsided.
options: A Guide to Choosing the Best Window for Plants
Turning Pots to Keep Growth Even
Why Plants Bend Toward the Light
How Plant Cells Divide
quests.correctAnswer: Why Plants Bend Toward the Light
quests.hint: Which title answers the question the passage raises in its opening sentence?
quests.explanation: Turning pots is a practical tip that follows. The passage mainly explains the reason behind the leaning.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice gives the cause and effect at the heart of the passage.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: When a shopping center opened outside town, Mr. Amin's small hardware store lost half its customers. He could not match the big store's prices, so he changed what he offered: repair advice, tool rentals, and delivery to elderly customers. Within a year, sales recovered, and neighbors began sending him friends.
options: Delivering Goods to Elderly Customers
Why Shopping Centers Are So Popular
How a Small Store Fought Back
Renting Tools to Neighbors
quests.correctAnswer: How a Small Store Fought Back
quests.hint: The store changes strategy in the middle. What triggered it?
quests.explanation: Tool rentals and deliveries are pieces of the new approach. The passage moves from the threat to the response and the recovery.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title includes the competition, the store's changes, and the recovery.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Open-plan offices make it easy for colleagues to ask a quick question or overhear useful news, and they cost less to build than rooms with walls. However, noise and interruptions make it difficult to concentrate on detailed work. Some companies now keep an open area for teamwork and a few quiet rooms for focus.
options: Building Offices Without Walls at a Lower Cost
Designing Quiet Rooms for Focus
How Colleagues Share News Quickly
The Trade-Offs of Open-Plan Offices
quests.correctAnswer: The Trade-Offs of Open-Plan Offices
quests.hint: How does the word 'however' change the passage?
quests.explanation: Lower cost and quiet rooms come from opposite halves of the passage. The best title reflects the trade-off between them.
quests.whyThisTitle: It represents both the advantages and the disadvantages of the layout.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: When the fire alarm rings, everyone stops what they are doing. Teachers count students and lead them along marked routes to the assembly point outside. Doors are closed behind them but not locked. Once everyone is counted, the fire warden reports to the office, and only after an all-clear signal do people return.
options: Why Fire Alarms Ring Loudly
How a School Fire Drill Works
Keeping Doors Closed in a Fire
Counting Students at the Assembly Point
quests.correctAnswer: How a School Fire Drill Works
quests.hint: Follow the actions from the alarm to the return.
quests.explanation: Counting and closing doors are moments inside the procedure. The passage lists what happens in order, from alarm to all-clear.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title covers the whole drill, not one of its steps.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: People often forget a name seconds after hearing it. The reason is usually not poor memory but divided attention: while being introduced, the listener is thinking about what to say next. The name never gets stored. Repeating it aloud and using it once or twice in conversation gives the brain a second chance to hold on to it.
options: Feeling Nervous at Introductions
Names That Slip Away
Improving Memory in General
Repeating a Name Aloud
quests.correctAnswer: Names That Slip Away
quests.hint: Ask what the passage explains and what it suggests doing about it.
quests.explanation: Repeating a name is only the remedy. General memory is too broad, since the passage says memory is not the real problem.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title covers the cause of forgetting and the fix in a single title.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: When a friend is upset, the urge to fix the problem is strong. But most people want to be heard first. Listen without interrupting, and reflect back what you heard so they know you understand. Offer advice only if they ask for it. Small gestures, such as sitting nearby or sending a message the next day, often matter more than clever words.
options: Sending Kind Messages the Next Day
Understanding Other People's Emotions
Giving Advice That Solves Problems
Listening to a Friend in Trouble
quests.correctAnswer: Listening to a Friend in Trouble
quests.hint: The opening sentence describes a common mistake. What does the rest of the passage recommend instead?
quests.explanation: The passage warns against rushing to fix things and recommends listening. Advice-giving is what the passage says to hold back.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title names the listening approach the passage recommends in place of quick fixes.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Farmers in dry regions face a constant problem: water evaporates before crops can use it. Drip irrigation delivers small amounts directly to plant roots through thin tubes, so almost none is wasted. Farms that switched have grown the same crops using far less water, and some have expanded onto land once considered too dry.
options: Why All Crops Need Water
Farming on Once-Dry Land
Thin Tubes That Reach Plant Roots
Drip Irrigation for Dry Farms
quests.correctAnswer: Drip Irrigation for Dry Farms
quests.hint: Ask what problem is stated and what technology answers it.
quests.explanation: The thin tubes and the newly farmed land are details of the solution and its results. The title has to connect the problem, the method, and the benefit.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice ties the dryness problem to the irrigation method and its gains.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: A guided walking tour and a hop-on bus tour show a city in very different ways. On foot, a group can enter small streets, hear stories at each corner, and stop for photographs, but it covers only a small area. A bus reaches distant sights and rests tired legs, though passengers see much of the city through a window. Many visitors choose a walking tour for the old center and a bus for the outskirts.
options: Two Ways to Tour a City
Finding Small Streets in Old Towns
Taking Photographs While Traveling
Resting Your Legs on a Bus
quests.correctAnswer: Two Ways to Tour a City
quests.hint: Look at how the passage balances each option, and how it ends.
quests.explanation: Resting legs and small streets are single points from each side. The passage sets both options side by side and ends by combining them.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title reflects the comparison and the practical conclusion that each has a best use.
